extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students studying patent trial procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing trials in patent-infringement actions: the respective roles of court and jury, when verdicts will be set aside or a new trial granted, standards for newly discovered evidence, writs of error, and taxation of costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury must follow the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The verdict of the jury must follow the evidence, not their private opinion apart from the evidence, and must be based on all the testimony offered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the verdict is manifestly the result of prejudice or error, or contrary to the court's instructions, or void for repugnancy or uncertainty, it will be set aside and a new trial ordered. The court will not interfere merely because it would have reached a different conclusion from the same premises, nor because the jury awarded larger damages than expected, unless the amount is palpably extravagant indicating corruption or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court defines legal questions; jury decides factual questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court defines legal attributes (e.g., construction of the patent, doctrine of estoppel, statute of limitations), while the jury determines factual matters (e.g., execution and authenticity of instruments, identity of parties, whether the accused device is the same as the claimed invention, whether acts constitute infringement, and computation of damages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court instructs on legal doctrines and the scope of claims; the jury applies those doctrines to the evidence. Either tribunal assuming the powers of the other on important matters is ground for error unless the parties have waived objection by treating the question as decided by that authority during trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions of infringement and complicity are jury issues of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the defendant's acts infringe the patent, whether an employee is responsible to obey employer commands, and what degree of complicity renders one liable when infringement is completed by others are questions for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court declares doctrines concerning infringement and liability; the jury decides whether the defendant's acts are true infringements according to those doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verdict void for repugnancy, uncertainty, prejudice or misdirection
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict will be set aside if it is the manifest result of prejudice or error, contrary to the court's instructions, or void for repugnancy or uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: verdicts evidently resulting from mistake, prejudice, or a regard for equities rather than law; repugnant or uncertain verdicts. A verdict against the evidence may be set aside where the preponderance is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial without a jury requires written stipulation; court may make general or special findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties or their attorneys may file a written stipulation to try issues of fact before the court without a jury; the court then determines law and fact, and its finding (general or special) occupies the same position as a jury verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A special finding resembles a special verdict and is reviewable by the Supreme Court. Statutory authority cited for trying issues without a jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for granting a new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts may grant new trials after a jury verdict for reasons that include errors committed by the court or jury during the trial or the discovery of new evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court errors: admitting improper evidence, rejecting admissible evidence, departing from the law in instructions, submitting questions of law to the jury (e.g., patent construction). Jury errors: misconduct, departing from law or evidence, verdict contrary to evidence, excessive damages. If the same facts were shown by proper testimony or evidence was immaterial, a motion for new trial will be refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper admission of evidence as ground for new trial (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The admission of improper evidence is generally a sufficient ground for a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: if the same facts were later shown by proper testimony, or the erroneous evidence was rendered immaterial by subsequent disclosures, or the objection was purely technical and the result would have been the same, the motion for a new trial may be refused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper rejection of evidence as ground for new trial (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The improper rejection of admissible evidence can be a ground for a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But if reception of the excluded evidence would have made no difference in the result, or its place was supplied by other testimony, exclusion will not be sufficient ground. The court will consider materiality and effect on outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misdirection in charge / submission of law to jury is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: An error in the court's charge to the jury, either by submitting a question of law to their decision or by misdirecting them on a material point, is fatal to the verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically, submission to the jury of questions of law such as the construction of the patent is ground for a new trial. Failure to give a requested instruction is not a ground if the charge as a whole covers the law correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury misconduct and oath-breaches warrant new trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct by any juror during the trial, or acts/omissions that involve a breach of the juror's oath, vitiate proceedings and may justify a new trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such misconduct may include bias, entering with a preformed conclusion, or other acts that affect impartiality; proof required but need not show the conduct certainly influenced the jury if it could have affected impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly discovered evidence standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A new trial may be granted for newly discovered evidence provided the evidence is material, not cumulative, will probably change the result, and could not have been known before or during the former trial by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence was known or discoverable earlier with due diligence, a new trial will be refused. Discovery by surprise affords no ground if the party could have requested a continuance but instead proceeded and thus waived the matter. Motions for new trial on new evidence must state in detail efforts made to obtain the evidence for the former trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of excepted errors not raised at trial
rubrics_metrics.description: Any error that came to the knowledge of the defeated party or counsel during the trial and was not excepted to at the time is thereby waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes or negligence of parties or counsel in preparing or attending to the case are not ground for new trial. A motion once denied cannot be repeated except on new facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for excessive damages and remittitur
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict awarding excessive damages may be set aside; where damages are merely excessive the error can be cured by entering a remititur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A verdict will not be set aside for excessive damages unless plainly and largely beyond the injury sustained. Nominal damages usually carry costs; excessive or palpably extravagant awards may indicate corruption or mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writ of error to Supreme Court — scope and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A writ of error lies to the Supreme Court from the judgment of a circuit court in any action at law for infringement; it is a matter of right and amount involved is immaterial if the error relates to a principle or rule of patent law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements: the judgment must be final; errors of law alone are reviewable and must appear on the record with exceptions duly taken; writ must issue within two years after entry of final judgment except where disability extends time; the entire record must be sent and matters claimed as error properly assigned or they will not be noticed. The Supreme Court may reverse, modify, or affirm and may award damages for delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors within judicial discretion are not reviewable on writ of error
rubrics_metrics.description: No writ of error lies from decisions on matters within the court's discretion (e.g., grant/refusal of continuance, grant/refusal of new trial, allowance or rejection of amendments), and certain costs decisions absent statutory thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: decisions on continuance, new trial, refusal/allowance of amendment, and costs (unless exceeding statutory amounts) are generally not reviewable as errors of law on writ of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule on costs in patent infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule, the party who recovers judgment in an action at law for infringement also recovers costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory provisions cited. However, important exceptions apply (see related metrics): disclaimers of excessive claims, abandonment of claims at trial, re-issue complications, suits solely for vindication, apportionment when multiple patents/claims involved, nominal damages, and conduct of parties may alter taxation of costs. Specifics include: (a) costs denied where excessive claim is cured by disclaimer pending suit or where certain claims abandoned at trial; (b) disclaimer filed without necessity or after verdict may allow costs; (c) nominal damages usually carry costs; (d) where plaintiff recovers on one of several claims and others are invalid and not disclaimed, costs may be denied or apportioned; (e) where suit is for judicial interpretation or vindication and defendant is not guilty of wilful wrong, costs may be denied against defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of disclaimers and multiple claims on costs
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent has several claims and some are excessive or invalid, the presence, timing, and necessity of disclaimers affect entitlement to costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If excessive claims are disclaimed before suit, costs may follow; disclaimer after verdict may give rise to new trial but not automatically affect verdict or costs. If valid claims are recovered but invalid claims not disclaimed, costs may be denied; if plaintiff recovers upon all claims (validity and novelty affirmed) costs follow. Where suit involves several patents or several claims with mixed results, costs may be apportioned or denied depending on outcomes and whether any unreasonable delay or unnecessary disclaimers occurred.
